Consider the mapping diagram of the function [MATH: f(x),] shown below.

Graphic:

Content:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/da0f7c4a868c8dde679865455ec74d77]

Content:
Now, we have a mapping diagram that "reverses" the action of the function [MATH: f.] The diagram itself represents a new function, which we call the inverse of the function [MATH: f,] and denote by [MATH: f^{-1}.]

Content:
We can evaluate the inverse function [MATH: f^{-1}] at any point in the range of [MATH: f.] For example, to find the value of [MATH: f^{-1}(2),] we notice that we have an arrow from [MATH: {\color{black}2}] (on the right) to [MATH: {\color{black}0}] (on the left). Therefore,
[MATH: f^{-1}({\color{black}2}) = {\color{black}0}.]

Content:
In the original function, [MATH: f,] that same arrow went from [MATH: {\color{black}0}] (on the left) to [MATH: {\color{black}2}] (on the right). So, we have that [MATH: f({\color{black}0})={\color{black}2},] and as a result, we obtain
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(0)) = 0.]
So, applying the function [MATH: f] and then "reversing" the action using [MATH: f^{-1}] will get us back to [MATH: 0.]

Content:
In general, this is true for every [MATH: x] in the domain of the function [MATH: f\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: f^{-1}(-1) = 4.]

items.title: The Definition of the Inverse Function

sections.normalized_html: Recall that the [MATH: f^{-1}] "reverses" the action of [MATH: f] so that [MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x,] which can be visualized using the mapping diagram, as shown below.
sections.readable_text:
Recall that the [MATH: f^{-1}] "reverses" the action of [MATH: f] so that
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x,]
which can be visualized using the mapping diagram, as shown below.
[IMG: /graphics/fb37131843cf52b9e2738d93f97a5590]

sections.normalized_html: Since [MATH: f^{-1}(f(x))] is just the composition [MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x),] we can now give the algebraic definition of the inverse.
sections.readable_text: Since [MATH: f^{-1}(f(x))] is just the composition [MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x),] we can now give the algebraic definition of the inverse.

sections.normalized_html: The function [MATH: f^{-1}] is called the inverse of the function [MATH: f] if [MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x] for each [MATH: x] in the domain of [MATH: f.]
sections.readable_text:
The function [MATH: f^{-1}] is called the inverse of the function [MATH: f] if
[MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x]
for each [MATH: x] in the domain of [MATH: f.]

sections.normalized_html: In other words, to show that two functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are inverses of each other, we need to check the following condition: [MATH: (g\circ f)(x) = x.]
sections.readable_text:
In other words, to show that two functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are inverses of each other, we need to check the following condition:
[MATH: (g\circ f)(x) = x.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that the [MATH: f^{-1}] "reverses" the action of [MATH: f] so that
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x,]
which can be visualized using the mapping diagram, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fb37131843cf52b9e2738d93f97a5590]

Content:
Since [MATH: f^{-1}(f(x))] is just the composition [MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x),] we can now give the algebraic definition of the inverse.

Content:
The function [MATH: f^{-1}] is called the inverse of the function [MATH: f] if
[MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x]
for each [MATH: x] in the domain of [MATH: f.]

Content:
In other words, to show that two functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are inverses of each other, we need to check the following condition:
[MATH: (g\circ f)(x) = x.]

items.title: Computing an Inverse Function Using the Definition

sections.normalized_html: Suppose that [MATH: f(x)=\dfrac{x}{4}-2] and [MATH: g(x)=4x-2k.] If [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] then what is the value of [MATH: k]?
sections.readable_text: Suppose that [MATH: f(x)=\dfrac{x}{4}-2] and [MATH: g(x)=4x-2k.] If [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] then what is the value of [MATH: k]?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] then we must have

[MATH: g(f(x)) = x.]

To find [MATH: g(f(x)),] we write down the function [MATH: g] and replace every occurrence of [MATH: x] with [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: g(x)|= 4x − 2k; g(f(x))|= 4f(x) − 2k]

Then, we substitute [MATH: {\color{blue}f(x)} = {\color{blue}\dfrac{x}{4}-2}] into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

[MATH: g(f(x))|= 4f(x) − 2k; = 4((x)/(4) − 2) − 2k; = x − 8 − 2k]

Because [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] we also know that [MATH: g(f(x)) = x.] Equating the above expression with [MATH: x] and solving for [MATH: k,] we get

[MATH: x − 8 − 2k|= x; x − 8 − 2k|= x; − 8 − 2k|= 0; 2k|= − 8; k|= − 4.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the mapping diagram of the function [MATH: f(x),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b075c5e399f2f0b3a3c7ae417ab52323]

Content:
Let's now reverse the arrows, as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/da0f7c4a868c8dde679865455ec74d77]

Content:
Now, we have a mapping diagram that "reverses" the action of the function [MATH: f.] The diagram itself represents a new function, which we call the inverse of the function [MATH: f,] and denote by [MATH: f^{-1}.]

Content:
We can evaluate the inverse function [MATH: f^{-1}] at any point in the range of [MATH: f.] For example, to find the value of [MATH: f^{-1}(2),] we notice that we have an arrow from [MATH: {\color{black}2}] (on the right) to [MATH: {\color{black}0}] (on the left). Therefore,
[MATH: f^{-1}({\color{black}2}) = {\color{black}0}.]

Content:
In the original function, [MATH: f,] that same arrow went from [MATH: {\color{black}0}] (on the left) to [MATH: {\color{black}2}] (on the right). So, we have that [MATH: f({\color{black}0})={\color{black}2},] and as a result, we obtain
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(0)) = 0.]
So, applying the function [MATH: f] and then "reversing" the action using [MATH: f^{-1}] will get us back to [MATH: 0.]

Content:
In general, this is true for every [MATH: x] in the domain of the function [MATH: f\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating an Inverse Function From a Mapping Diagram

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/70abac9cf00204ab68516f21c84ac94c]

The function [MATH: f(x)] is represented by the mapping diagram above. What is [MATH: f^{-1}(-1)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Method 1

The function [MATH: f^{-1}(x)] reverses the action of [MATH: f(x),] as depicted below.

[IMG: /graphics/1df2bc501dc85c96976727ba0c4e2546]

From the above, we see that [MATH: f^{-1}(-1) = 4.]

Method 2

From the given mapping diagram, we have

[MATH: f(4) = -1.]

Applying [MATH: f^{-1}] to both sides of the above equation, and using the fact that [MATH: f^{-1}\left(f(x)\right) = x,] we get

[MATH: f^{− 1}(f(4))|= f^{− 1}(− 1); 4|= f^{− 1}(− 1).]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: f^{-1}(-1) = 4.]

Therefore, we conclude that [MATH: f^{-1}(3) = -4.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Definition of the Inverse Function

Content:
Recall that the [MATH: f^{-1}] "reverses" the action of [MATH: f] so that
[MATH: f^{-1}(f(x)) = x,]
which can be visualized using the mapping diagram, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fb37131843cf52b9e2738d93f97a5590]

Content:
Since [MATH: f^{-1}(f(x))] is just the composition [MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x),] we can now give the algebraic definition of the inverse.

Content:
The function [MATH: f^{-1}] is called the inverse of the function [MATH: f] if
[MATH: (f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x]
for each [MATH: x] in the domain of [MATH: f.]

Content:
In other words, to show that two functions [MATH: f(x)] and [MATH: g(x)] are inverses of each other, we need to check the following condition:
[MATH: (g\circ f)(x) = x.]

---

Item 12 — Example: Computing an Inverse Function Using the Definition

Example Prompt:
Suppose that [MATH: f(x)=\dfrac{x}{4}-2] and [MATH: g(x)=4x-2k.] If [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] then what is the value of [MATH: k]?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] then we must have

[MATH: g(f(x)) = x.]

To find [MATH: g(f(x)),] we write down the function [MATH: g] and replace every occurrence of [MATH: x] with [MATH: f(x)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: g(x)|= 4x − 2k; g(f(x))|= 4f(x) − 2k]

Then, we substitute [MATH: {\color{blue}f(x)} = {\color{blue}\dfrac{x}{4}-2}] into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

[MATH: g(f(x))|= 4f(x) − 2k; = 4((x)/(4) − 2) − 2k; = x − 8 − 2k]

Because [MATH: g] is the inverse of [MATH: f,] we also know that [MATH: g(f(x)) = x.] Equating the above expression with [MATH: x] and solving for [MATH: k,] we get

[MATH: x − 8 − 2k|= x; x − 8 − 2k|= x; − 8 − 2k|= 0; 2k|= − 8; k|= − 4.]
